title: The Southward Offensive
subtitle: A Desna crossing threatens the rear of the Soviet armies in Ukraine
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: A bridge at Novgorod-Seversky opened the way behind the Soviet Dnieper defence. The response exposed the difficulty of moving armies, supplies and civilian labour while German occupation violence escalated farther west.
body:
A crossing changes the problem

On 26 August 1941, the 3rd Panzer Division gained a usable bridge across the Desna at Novgorod-Seversky (now Novhorod-Siverskyi). Beyond it lay the communications of the Soviet armies defending Ukraine. Those armies still faced principally westward along the Dnieper; Guderian’s troops could now advance south behind them. The bridge mattered because tanks, infantry and supply columns could cross it together, turning a local penetration into a threat to an entire front. Soviet headquarters acknowledged the loss of the town in its report the following morning. Its order of 29 August identified the breach on the left of the 13th Army and sought to strike back. The Germans had opened a route. The Soviet command still had an opportunity to close it. [1]

The crossing put into practice the southward turn examined in The Decision to Turn South. Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group and Weichs’s 2nd Army were moving from Army Group Centre’s southern wing as other formations took over their positions. Rundstedt’s Army Group South was still fighting along the Dnieper. For the two forces to cooperate, separate crossings and advances had to succeed. Kiev was not yet encircled on 26 August, and the southern pincer had not begun its decisive movement north.[2]

The starting problem was the survival of substantial Soviet forces after two months of retreat. David Stahel’s study of Kiev emphasises that the German victory later associated with this campaign emerged from an army already experiencing serious attrition. Army Group South had failed to dispose of the Southwestern Front through its own opening operations, while its motorised formations had accumulated losses and mechanical wear. Assistance from the north offered a way around resistance that frontal pressure had not removed. This interpretation gives the campaign a more demanding explanation than the familiar image of an effortless armoured sweep: German operational opportunity and German material weakness developed together. The southward offensive attempted to exploit the former before the latter made another major undertaking impossible. [3]a

For Soviet commanders, the threat was more complicated than an approaching column. The Germans were moving near the junction between two fronts, the large Soviet commands responsible for several armies. Holding a river line depended on neighbouring formations remaining in contact, reporting promptly and sharing a workable understanding of the enemy’s direction. The fighting now tested all three conditions. It also exposed a difficult choice: divisions moved north to protect the flank would be unavailable along the Dnieper, where the Germans were preparing crossings of their own. The Soviet response was therefore an attempt to preserve an entire connected defensive system while its northern attachment was coming under attack. [4]b

The offensive’s unequal moving parts

Guderian’s account places the opening movement on 25 August. XXIV Motorised Corps sent the 3rd Panzer Division towards Novgorod-Seversky, with the 10th Motorised Division moving through Kholmy and Avdeyevka. The 4th Panzer Division first had to finish fighting near the Sudost before following. XLVII Motorised Corps protected the eastern flank. By the evening of 26 August, the 3rd Panzer Division was at the Desna crossing, whereas the 4th remained engaged southeast of Starodub and the 17th Panzer Division fought near Semtsy, south of Pochep. These dispositions describe an offensive assembling through combat, rather than a compact formation already moving at a single speed. [5]

Guderian’s leading tanks represented only part of his command. A panzer group combined armoured and motorised formations with artillery, engineers and supporting services; the whole organisation had to sustain the penetration. The American Army’s operational history describes substantial strength left to contain Bryansk Front. Those formations protected the advance but could not simultaneously reinforce its spearhead. Soviet resistance beside the German route therefore mattered even when it failed to stop the leading division. It obliged Guderian to divide the force with which he hoped to turn the Soviet position. [2]

Infantry armies performed a related but different task. Weichs’s 2nd Army approached the northern side of the Ukrainian theatre after the fighting around Gomel. Its progress brought pressure against Soviet formations that might otherwise have turned against Guderian’s western flank. Yet infantry could not simply reproduce the movement of selected motorised detachments. It had its own defended routes to open, artillery to bring forward and marching columns to supply. A successful armoured advance could thus increase the distance between the spearhead and the infantry expected to make its gains secure. The operational relationship was reciprocal: the tanks created a threat deep in the Soviet rear, while the infantry helped prevent that threat from becoming an isolated excursion. [2]c

The Soviet command structure was changing during the breakthrough. An order issued at 18.00 on 25 August transferred Central Front’s forces to Bryansk Front from midnight at the beginning of 26 August; some of its new army arrangements would take effect on 28 August. Andrei Yeremenko’s headquarters had to absorb those formations while directing a battle across the same area. Reports, supply relationships and subordinate staffs all needed to be connected to the new command before they could work together.[1]

The evening report for 26 August shows how unevenly that process worked. Communications with 50th Army functioned by telephone, telegraph and liaison officers; the telegraph and radio connections with 13th Army were intermittent. An operational group was being established around Khutor-Mikhailovsky to control forces inherited from Central Front. These details help explain why a headquarters could possess a strategic appreciation of danger without possessing an accurate, timely picture of every threatened crossing. Recognising the danger was only the beginning of a response. A report had to reach headquarters, produce an order suited to the forces available, and return through the damaged communications network before the threatened formation’s position changed again. [1]d

Rivers, roads and the new Soviet flank

The Desna, Seym and Dnieper formed connected obstacles rather than three interchangeable blue lines. The Desna approached the Dnieper from the northeast, while the Seym fed into the Desna farther upstream. A German advance from the Starodub region towards the rear of the Southwestern Front therefore encountered successive river valleys and a limited set of useful crossings. Securing one passage did not provide an uninterrupted road to Kiev’s eastern communications. It changed the next military problem: Soviet forces could contest the bridgehead, threaten its approaches or hold another river farther south. The Southwestern Front’s orders consequently identified routes towards Krolevets, Vorozhba and Konotop, as well as stretches of riverbank. The command was trying to protect a network through which the enemy could penetrate. [4]

The new 40th Army was intended to secure this northern flank. Assigned to Southwestern Front on 26 August under Kuzma Podlas, it was given headquarters at Konotop and responsibility for preventing a breakthrough towards the routes behind the Dnieper defence. The detailed directive of 28 August listed the 293rd and 135th Rifle Divisions, 10th Tank Division, 2nd Airborne Corps and 5th Antitank Artillery Brigade among its forces. These assignments established a defensive task; the formations still had to assemble with the weapons and communications needed to perform it.[4]

The airborne corps were being employed as ground troops. Elements of the 2nd were to travel by truck to the Korop–Maloye Ustye sector, while the 3rd was ordered to concentrate around Konotop by the morning of 31 August. Their value here lay in organised infantry that could be moved towards the breach. Getting them there depended on road transport and time, rather than a parachute landing.[4]e

The same directive required the 5th Army to continue holding the Dnieper while protecting itself against attack from the north. At least one division was to defend a specified stretch of the Desna by the end of 29 August; at least two divisions were to be retained near the junction with 40th Army. The 37th Army had to hold Kiev, with its flanks tied to the Dnieper and its centre occupying the fortified approaches west of the city. The 26th and 38th Armies continued the defence farther south. Each instruction was intelligible in isolation. Together they reveal the strain of trying to preserve a long river front while constructing a second front at an angle to it. [4]

Nor was every formation immediately available for the task assigned to it. The document placed the 304th Rifle Division in reserve while it completed its armament and left the 81st Rifle Division reorganising around Lubny. Such details correct the impression created by orderly symbols on a situation map. A division could exist in an order of battle while still requiring weapons, replacement personnel or reorganisation before effective employment. The northern defence was therefore a race between the German advance and the Soviet ability to turn administrative assignments into coordinated fighting power. That race remained open at the end of August; its outcome should not be read backward from the catastrophe of September. [4]f

Resistance that consumed the advance

The Bryansk Front reports show local resistance continuing beside the German breakthrough. At Semtsy, south of Pochep, the Germans attacked after repeated air bombardment and took the settlement during the afternoon of 26 August. The following morning’s Soviet report stated that a counterattack had recovered it at 22.00. These are headquarters reports, not a complete reconstruction of the engagement, but their sequence is revealing. On the same day that the Germans gained a major crossing farther south, a nearby sector was changing hands through attack and counterattack. The front was not dissolving uniformly. Its unevenness forced German commanders to decide where to press ahead and where to employ troops that might otherwise have joined the main thrust. [1]g

By 29 August, Yeremenko had ordered a mobile group under Arkady Yermakov to attack towards the threatened sector. The grouping combined the 108th Tank Division, 141st Tank Brigade and 4th Cavalry Division. The order prescribed separate routes, Sudost crossings and successive objectives, with the intended arrival around Novgorod-Seversky by the end of 31 August. The cavalry was to follow behind the tank formations and cooperate in destroying the opposing forces. This was an effort to strike the side of the penetration and restore the connection between Soviet armies. Its existence establishes a deliberate response; the ambitious deadlines establish the command’s expectations, not proof that the objectives were reached. [1]

The counterstroke also needed air and ground units to stay in contact. The air command was ordered to protect the march and river crossings, support the attacks, and send an operational officer and a U-2 aircraft to each principal armoured formation. A radio centre was to be established near Trubchevsk. These practical arrangements addressed the problem of locating friendly troops and directing support where it was needed. They show what headquarters was trying to organise; they do not establish that every part of the scheme worked.[1]h

A minefield on the wrong side of the report

Three T-40 light tanks of the 108th Tank Division entered a Soviet minefield while reconnoitring near Sloboda on 26 August. Bryansk Front’s report recorded a lieutenant killed, a soldier wounded and two tanks put out of action. It supplied no names and did not explain how the reconnaissance party had missed the minefield’s location. The incident shows the immediate cost when information about defensive preparations failed to reach friendly troops moving through them.[1]i

Moving supplies and making roads

Bryansk Front’s rear-services directive of 25 August set out the supply system its response would require. It assigned railway sections through Bryansk and the approaches from Orel and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky, and prescribed ammunition reserves with troops, at army depots and at front bases. Food and fodder were also to be stocked at successive levels, including fifteen days at front bases. These were requirements to be met as armies regrouped and counterattacked, rather than an inventory proving that every reserve was already in place.[1]

Every army was also to have at least two prepared roads suitable for motor and horse transport. Roads and bridges were to remain passable in different weather conditions, and local road authorities and the civilian population were to be used extensively to bring them into condition. Difficult stretches required traffic regulation and tractors ready to assist vehicles. The plan was due on the evening of 26 August, with the road preparations to be completed by 1 September. These deadlines placed repair work inside the battle’s timetable. A formation moving towards the Desna could be delayed by a damaged bridge or an obstructed approach even when its headquarters had fuel somewhere in the rear. [1]

The directive placed civilian labour inside the supply plan. Local road authorities and inhabitants were to help make the routes usable, alongside military arrangements for traffic control and vehicle recovery. It does not establish how particular villages recruited workers, whether they volunteered or were compelled, or what protection their households received. The documented demand is nevertheless substantial: headquarters required civilian work on a fixed military deadline while the front was moving. This was one way the army’s effort to recover imposed duties on people behind it. The record counts the roads to be prepared; it leaves the workers’ individual circumstances largely unrecorded. [1]

Medical evacuation ran in the opposite direction. The directive provided for wounded and sick personnel to move by hospital trains from Bryansk and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky towards the evacuation system around Orel, Livny, Yelets and Mtsensk. It also required army medical facilities to be organised near the principal rail connections. This was a planned chain of movement from fighting units to transport and onward treatment. Its dependence on rail access explains another consequence of the German penetration: a threatened communications route endangered both the arrival of ammunition and the removal of casualties. Holding a junction could preserve the possibility of care as well as the capacity to continue fighting. [1]j

German mobility depended on a similarly layered system, although one increasingly stretched away from its original bases. Fuel delivered to the theatre still had to reach the divisions; replacement parts still had to reach repair personnel; damaged vehicles still had to be recovered. The German Army’s early September assessment, summarised in its postwar American study, reported exhausted fuel stockpiles and shortages that sometimes interrupted operations in the south. Its 4 September tank assessment distinguished vehicles available for employment from those under repair and those disabled. Those later figures cannot describe every division on 26 August, but they confirm that the turn south was being executed during an accumulating maintenance problem, before autumn weather could provide an all-purpose explanation for German difficulties. [6]k

Grossman’s road out of the retreat

Vasily Grossman recorded the retreat as a Soviet correspondent travelling among soldiers and displaced families. His notebooks notice an older woman waiting for her son beside a passing column, people offering food, abandoned homes and roads shared by refugees, livestock and military vehicles. The observations span his August–September journey and cannot all be assigned to 26 August. They show people searching for relatives, helping strangers and deciding what they could carry while the armies moved through their lives. The surviving selection was edited and translated after the war.[7]l

The southern front and the wider war

Farther south, Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group was still involved in the struggle for the Dnieper approaches. Southern Front’s report covering 15–31 August described combat around Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Berislav and Kherson, alongside the regrouping and replenishment of Soviet formations. Its account dated the evacuation of Dnepropetrovsk to the early hours of 25 August, after sustained fighting on the approaches. These operations had their own objectives: crossings towards the industrial districts farther east, and approaches towards the Crimea in the lower river sector. They were not yet the northward movement from Kremenchuk that would later form the southern arm of the Kiev encirclement. [8]

The lower river remained actively contested. A Soviet attempt to regain Kherson on 24 August failed; the same summary described renewed German pressure at Berislav on 26 August and the Soviet withdrawal across the river during the following night. On 30 August German troops established a foothold around Kakhovka after artillery and air preparation. These developments show why it is misleading to imagine Army Group South waiting in readiness for Guderian. Its formations were fighting their way through a broad river system against opponents still capable of resistance and counterattack. The later concentration for the decisive encirclement would require selection among these competing tasks. [8]m

Western policy operated on another timescale. In the Roosevelt–Churchill message transmitted officially to Moscow on 18 August, the two leaders proposed a conference to determine longer-term Soviet requirements and the allocation of shared resources. They promised continuing shipments while acknowledging that British and American resources, although large, had competing demands. This correspondence matters because it records a developing commitment to Soviet survival without implying that promised equipment was already available to Podlas or Yeremenko. A shipment leaving a Western port and a weapon reaching a threatened division were separate events, connected by voyages, unloading, assembly and onward transport. The immediate defence of the Desna still depended on the forces and material that Soviet commanders could bring into the battle at hand. [9]n

Children beyond the operational map

Isaac Piatsetski, a Polish Jewish refugee interviewed in 1998, remembered seeing a train evacuate children from Bila Tserkva before German occupation. Doris Bergen places his account alongside the August murder of Jewish children there and the later testimony of German chaplains who had tried to intervene. She distinguishes Piatsetski’s recollection of the departure from his less secure belief about the train’s eventual destination. His testimony preserves an attempt to get children out while routes remained open, and connects the displacement that began in Poland in 1939 with the danger now reaching Soviet Ukraine.[10]o

Farther west, conquest was already exposing entire communities to organised murder. At Kamenets-Podolsk, now Kamianets-Podilskyi, German killing units and forces under Higher SS and Police Leader Friedrich Jeckeln murdered Jewish residents and Jews deported from Hungary. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the massacre to 26–28 August and identifies 23,600 as Jeckeln’s reported total. That figure belongs to the whole action, not to 26 August alone. Hungarian authorities had expelled people classified as foreign Jews, including people unable to prove Hungarian citizenship; German authorities then held them in occupied territory. The victims included families, not simply the adult men whom earlier German killings had often targeted. Deportation and murder were connected decisions by identifiable authorities. This escalation occurred while German armies were still fighting for the crossings farther east, and before Kiev had fallen. [11]p

The position reached

By the end of 26 August, the Germans had gained a significant crossing and Soviet headquarters faced an urgent threat to the northern connection of the Ukrainian defence. They had not yet converted that opportunity into a closed pocket. The Soviet orders of the following days show additional formations being assigned, river sectors being reinforced and a counterstroke being organised against the penetration. They also expose the limits of that response: incomplete concentrations, formations still reorganising, interrupted communications and a transport system required to support several urgent purposes at once. The Germans benefited from those weaknesses while encountering enough resistance to consume strength along their expanding flanks. [1][4]

The crossing forced Soviet headquarters to defend two directions at once. Divisions needed along the Dnieper were also needed on the northern flank; trucks carrying them competed with supply and medical transport. The following days would test whether those movements could restore a connected defence before the Germans pushed farther south. In the north, a different evacuation crisis was already unfolding. The Baltic Withdrawal follows the ships leaving Tallinn, the units they carried and the passengers for whom survival did not necessarily mean arrival at a Soviet port.
